scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants the value of guidance while arguing electives should stay and doubting the reason; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Students often feel both freed and confused when handed a long list of course choices.
One claim holds that colleges should require all courses and eliminate electives, on the reason that people generally prefer following directions to making their own decisions.
I agree that clear guidance helps students, but I disagree that electives should be eliminated, and I doubt the reason behind the claim.

sections.role: Body 1 — The value of clear guidance

sentences.text: First, there is some value in giving students clear guidance about what to study.
A few required courses ensure that every student gains the most essential knowledge and skills.
For example, requiring basic writing and reasoning helps students in almost any later field.
This shows that some structure can protect students from leaving dangerous gaps in their learning.
Too much choice can indeed overwhelm students who do not yet know what they need.
Sensible requirements can give a degree a clear shape and purpose.
To this extent, some required courses are genuinely useful.
Second, however, eliminating electives entirely would be a serious mistake.
Electives let students explore their own interests and discover what they truly love.
Consider a student who finds her future career only because an elective sparked a new passion.
Such cases show that free choice can lead to growth that no fixed list could provide.
The reason behind the claim is also doubtful, since people often value making their own decisions.
Learning to choose wisely is itself an important part of becoming an educated adult.
Electives, then, should be kept alongside a sensible core of required courses.
In conclusion, a clear core of required courses can helpfully guide students.
But eliminating electives would rob students of choice, discovery, and growth.
The best colleges combine sensible requirements with the freedom that electives provide.
